analysis.one_liner: Bars debt collectors from texting or emailing consumers without their consent.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would require debt collectors to get consent before texting or emailing consumers, was introduced in March 2021 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act so debt collectors cannot email or text a consumer without the consumer's consent, after consent is withdrawn, or more often than the consumer agreed to. It would bar the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau from issuing debt-collection rules that allow unlimited emails or texts, require collectors to get consent directly from consumers before using any contact method besides mail or phone, let consumers opt out of any contact method, and require the CFPB to report on debt-collection complaints and enforcement actions.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers with debts in collection, who today can be deluged with emails and texts they never agreed to. Anyone who has had a debt sent to a collector could control how they are contacted — mail or phone, with the ability to say no to emails and texts and to change their mind at any time. Millions of Americans have debts in collection, so this would touch a very large number of households.

how_it_helps.text: Adds electronic contact without consent, after consent is withdrawn, or more often than agreed, to the list of prohibited debt-collection practices under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act.

Prohibits the CFPB from issuing any debt-collection rule that lets a collector send unlimited emails and texts to a consumer, and requires rules to obtain consumer consent directly before non-mail, non-phone contact and to let consumers opt out of any contact method.

Requires the CFPB to report semiannually on debt-collection complaints with a state-by-state breakdown and a list of enforcement actions against collectors, and to analyze the impact of electronic collection communications on consumers.

analysis.who_pays: Debt collection firms would bear the cost. They would have to obtain and track consent for electronic contact, honor opt-outs, and could not rely on high-volume automated emailing and texting to chase debts, which would raise their cost per account and shrink a contact channel they had begun using at scale.

drawbacks.text: Restricting email and text contact could push collections back to postal mail and phone calls, channels that are slower and more expensive and that some consumers may find less convenient than digital contact for resolving or disputing a debt.

Tying the CFPB's hands on debt-collection rules could block updates to decades-old rules; collectors argue that clear federal rules for electronic contact, rather than new bans, would benefit both sides by spelling out what is allowed.
Higher collection costs are ultimately passed through the credit system, which can show up in prices and credit terms for all borrowers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protection is straightforward and directly responsive to a well-documented problem: debt collectors flooding people with unwanted emails and texts. The main trade-off is that some consumers who would actually prefer digital contact lose that channel unless they affirmatively opt in, and collection costs could rise slightly. On balance the consent-and-opt-out design leaves consumers in charge of the trade-off, which is why the cost side is modest relative to the benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the same day in March 2021, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Ayanna Pressley introduced the Ending Debt Collection Harassment Act of 2021 on March 8, 2021, joined by Reps. Tlaib, Adams, Ocasio-Cortez, and Garcia of Illinois.

The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day, and the action record shows no further steps — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — for the remainder of the 117th Congress.

The bill would have prohibited debt collectors from emailing or texting a consumer without consent, barred the CFPB from issuing rules allowing unlimited electronic collection communications, and required CFPB reporting on debt-collection complaints and enforcement actions.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Debt collection firms are better off because the bill never advanced: they keep the ability to contact consumers electronically without first getting consent, and the status quo of heavy electronic collection contact continues.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Debt collection firms and their investors

for.name: Ayanna Pressley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it through introduction.

for.name: Rashida Tlaib, Alma Adams, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and Jesús García
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors of the bill at introduction.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Maxine Waters (D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 8, 2021 and never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, but the bill never got a hearing or vote, so no Republican position on it was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would end their ability to email and text consumers at will, requiring consent and honoring opt-outs, which raises their cost per account and shrinks their most efficient contact channel. Their interest in keeping unlimited electronic contact runs directly against consumers' interest in being left alone.

industries.industry: Creditors and lenders that sell or assign overdue debt
industries.note: They rely on collection agencies to recover unpaid balances; restrictions on electronic contact could slow recoveries slightly, but consumers who owe them money are the direct beneficiaries. The effect on creditors is modest either way.
